### ‘It’s a risk’: How Rockstar built the most detailed (and romantic) GTA yet
- Canonical URL: https://ainewsradar.xyz/news/94069e6d6514a6f7
- Primary Source: The Verge (https://www.theverge.com/entertainment/1035806/grand-theft-auto-6-rob-nelson-interview)
- Executive Summary: Rob Nelson, co-studio head at Rockstar North, confirmed that GTA 6 introduces an emotional narrative dimension through protagonists Jason and Lucia, set within a vast open world modeled on extensive field research in Florida (Leonida). The game aims to balance traditional criminal action with immersive, player-driven relational dynamics.
- Key Verified Facts:
* [Core Event] Rob Nelson (Co-studio head at Rockstar North, Producer of GTA 6): Integration of dual-protagonist relationship mechanics and the Leonida region as the core narrative anchor
* [Root Cause & Mechanism] To evolve the open-world paradigm by layering emotional progression over traditional systemic criminal gameplay
* [Key Fact Detail] Narrative innovation driven by the emotional bond between dual protagonists.
* [Key Position & Outlook] Dual-track design balancing traditional crime action and immersive interaction.
- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> Grand Theft Auto VI isn’t just the biggest GTA game to date; it’s also the most romantic. Though the series is well known for its sordid assortment of criminal leads, GTA VI switches things up by starring a pair of thieves who also happen to fall in love after meeting while stealing a car. It’s still an open-world action game full of chaos and mayhem. But many players will also be attempting to nurture the budding relationship in between heists. The sprawling game is designed to support both audiences.
> “It’s a risk,” explains Rob Nelson, producer on GTA VI and co-studio head at developer Rockstar North. “It’s a real change for Grand Theft Auto. You can still play it the old way, you can reject all of this stuff. But for people who do engage, it’s meaningful — you’re earning it, you’re working at it, just like in a normal relationship.”
> Despite the couple — named Jason and Lucia — being so central to the GTA VI experience, the development of the game didn’t start with characters or story. It began with a place. Nelson says that “pretty quickly” the team settled on placing the game in Leonida, the GTA universe’s version of Florida and the setting of one of the series’ most iconic games, Vice City on the PS2. In 2015, a small group of developers from Rockstar headed to Florida to get a sense of the place and set the groundwork for what would go on to become GTA VI.
> “We just went around to feel it out,” explains Nelson. “Go to the Everglades, go to the Keys, go to the city, as many places as we can, and start thinking about what aspects of the place we want to incorporate. And then the map team starts building our version of that and talking very loosely and very broadly about what types of people we want to include and what types of places.”
> The team realized they wanted to tell a story that would pull players through the various locations they were creating. And the best way to do that was to have characters who were relatively small-time criminals. They would start near the bottom of the criminal underworld and work their way up, traversing Leonida’s various locations, culminating in the splashy Vice City.
> At the same time, the developers also wanted to do something different with the character-switching mechanic from GTA V, which let players swap between three unique criminals, each with very different stories and motivations. For GTA VI, a couple working together to steal enough money to escape the outlaw life fit both of these ideas perfectly. But it also presented some new challenges.
> “Could we make a relationship work?” Nelson remembers thinking. “It’d be very different from three characters living separate lives that come together for narrative purposes and then split. These two are going to need to be together all the time and that’s going to be a challenge. It felt really wrong to have these people that are supposedly together only be together when we’re giving you scripted content.”
> While GTA V is the obvious reference point, the new GTA also builds off of Rockstar’s 2018 Western Red Dead Redemption 2. That game was notable in particular for giving players more ways to interact with the world: You could talk to any NPC, sit around a campfire while drinking coffee or playing cards, or grow out your beard for a new look.
> GTA VI expands this in ways that are designed to reinforce the relationship aspect of the experience. For instance, not only can you drink coffee, but you can also make a cup and hand it to your partner. The two can spend time together sitting on the couch watching TV, or go out to a club and dance. There’s even a button dedicated exclusively to making Jason and Lucia hold hands when they’re together.
> “If it’s additive, and it makes you laugh, we include it.”
> Nelson notes that when the team implemented the hand-holding feature, it was a revelatory moment for showing how the story and gameplay could connect. “When we got that mechanic in — and it’s not just a toggle, it’s an active thing that you have to commit to and hold — it was a really profound thing,” he says.
> But it’s also a careful balancing act. While RDR2 was a widely praised game, it also received criticism for its slow pace, which was due in large part to all of the small mechanical details. These added animations and button prompts that gave texture to the world but could also lead to a plodding pace. That would be a much bigger problem in a game like GTA, which is built around action. Nelson says that he can be “freakishly obsessive” about these kinds of details, but he and the team had to learn to let go when realism got in the way of the game itself.
> “Maybe you don’t have to carry around antifreeze in your trunk so that if your engine starts smoking you can top it up,” he says. “Certain things fall by the wayside in developing the game, where it’s like, we don’t need this. But other things, like eating food, it was important for us. You want to feel like you are this person existing in this world to a degree. That felt like it was additive. I love walking down the street with a beer and a cigarette and switching between the two, feeling like a dude. If it’s additive, and it makes you laugh, we include it.”
> This also led the team down some unexpected paths. For instance, GTA VI is the first game in the series with functioning bedsheets. In past titles, and in basically every other video game, characters simply lay on top of a bed to go to sleep. That’s because it’s a lot of effort to both animate a character going under the covers as well as rig the sheets so that characters can interact with them in a way that looks and feels natural. The payoff isn’t worth it. But in the context of GTA VI, where the characters hide out together in everything from dingy motel rooms to fancy hotels, it made sense to actually build it.
> “Because you’re sharing a living space, and you come in and see your partner sleeping at 3AM, it’s weird to see them laying on the top of the bed all the time,” Nelson says. “Nobody does that. It’s a lot of work to rig the covers on all of the different beds and have them both be able to get in and out of it and be able to be under the covers together.”
> Bedsheets, holding hands, cups of coffee — they’re seemingly small details in a world as large as Grand Theft Auto VI, one that encourages players to run wild. But they’re also indicative of the approach Rockstar took with this latest GTA and how the studio attempted to make every element work in concert, even if it required a lot of extra work, like the bed covers. “That’s an example of something that was a lot of work, but it was worth it.”

### Grand Theft Auto VI Is a Masterpiece
- Canonical URL: https://ainewsradar.xyz/news/5c1db2259346bf51
- Primary Source: Bloomberg (https://www.bloomberg.com/news/features/2026-11-18/gta-6-review-rockstar-games-latest-is-a-masterpiece?accessToken=eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJzb3VyY2UiOiJTdWJzY3JpYmVyR2lmdGVkQXJ0aWNsZSIsImlhdCI6MTc5NDk5OTYzNCwiZXhwIjoxNzk1NjA0NDM0LCJhcnRpY2xlSWQiOiJUT1AyS0hLR0lGUTgwMCIsImJjb25uZWN0SWQiOiJCMUVBQkI5NjQ2QUM0REZFQTJBRkI4MjI1MzgyQTJFQSJ9.pks5MCyquJRoPSiA_59TfyguHaO8mfXluOkX8OZaVSY)
- Executive Summary: Grand Theft Auto VI, developed by Rockstar Games, has received critical acclaim for its immersive open-world design and complex narrative. Centered in the fictional state of 'Leonida', the game utilizes a dual-protagonist structure (Jason and Lucia) to deliver a highly detailed and emotionally resonant interactive crime experience.
- Key Verified Facts:
* [Core Event] Rockstar Games (Fictional map 'Leonida): Released open-world game featuring dual-protagonist narrative
* [Root Cause & Mechanism] Exploring deep storytelling and high-fidelity interaction
* [Key Fact Detail] Dual-protagonist mechanics driving narrative depth.
* [Key Position & Outlook] Redefining AAA open-world interaction standards.
- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> The women can be as violent, visibly tough and deeply messed-up as the men … Jason and Lucia in Grand Theft Auto VI. Photograph: Rockstar Games View image in fullscreen The women can be as violent, visibly tough and deeply messed-up as the men … Jason and Lucia in Grand Theft Auto VI. Photograph: Rockstar Games ReviewGrand Theft Auto VI review – gaming’s most depraved world is now also its greatest love story With realism that defies belief, this vast game easily accommodates its trademark foulmouthed, OTT chaos – as well as new empathy for the fugitive couple at its centre
> Keza MacDonaldWed 18 Nov 2026 06.00 ESTLast modified on Wed 18 Nov 2026 06.03 ESTShare Prefer the Guardian on Google In GTA VI, Rockstar has created the most extraordinarily, indulgently detailed virtual world that we have yet seen. Reviewing it feels a bit like trying to review, say, Paris: it contains so many potential experiences that it’s hard to know where to start. If you had been spying on me playing this game over the past few weeks you may well have caught me robbing banks, shooting up a weed farm or tearing along the highway at sunset blaring Bad Bunny on the in-game radio, but you might equally have caught me doing squats at the gym, shopping, assembling a coffee table or walking along the beach eating ice-cream. There is such a multiplicity of things on offer here that it is difficult to nail down what this game definitively is. Is it an interactive crime movie? A city simulator? A driving game? A sort of absurdly expansive version of The Sims in which the people you’re dressing up and looking after just happen to be professional criminals? It will be different for everyone – that is the beauty of it.
> For me, though, this game is about Jason and Lucia, the fugitive couple through whom you experience all that Leonida has to offer. Jason is muscular, handsome, ex-military, steady and unflappable, sincere but spare with words. Lucia has been boosting cars since the age of 14, has a wicked sense of humour and takes zero bullshit. (Lucia is the scarier one; I found myself turning much more quickly to violence when playing as her.) At the start, Lucia is incarcerated and Jason is making a go of things in the sunbeaten Keys, working for a dodgy guy down on the marina and renting a run-down house on stilts with a jetty round the back and a pet snake. When Lucia gets out of prison, the two of them try to make some kind of life for themselves – but before long they get caught up with the wrong people and have to flee the cosy life they’ve just started building.
> For a long time you really are two-bit criminals on the run, getting in with every dirtbag petty thief and drug-runner you come across in order to scrape some cash together and stay under the radar. You meet hillbilly pill-heads and biker gangs, friendly conspiracy theorists, a shady doctor, Lucia’s former prison friends and their lowlife boyfriends. By the time I actually got to Vice City – a glitzy den of sin, the centre of all Leonida’s pleasures and all its most extravagant criminality, where the gangbangers hustle on social media and even the narcos are obsessed with their Instagram clout – I had been playing for 30 hours. It took me 70 hours to finish the game and I could have taken longer.
> Leonida is so lifelike that at times it beggars belief, so vast that it feels overwhelming, and outside the story missions you can do whatever you please. There are nightclubs, gyms, flea markets, malls, restaurants, clothes shops, basketball courts, shooting ranges, aircraft hangars, projects and mansions, places to hunt and fish or go kayaking, gas stations and thousands of individuals engaged in conversation as you pass by. Interesting things are always happening in your peripheral vision. You might witness the cops chasing someone down to plant drugs on them, or overhear an interesting confrontation, or see a car speeding away and wonder where it’s going – though interesting things always seemed to happen when I was driving a stolen car at high speed towards a discerning buyer, or otherwise unable to stop and follow my nose. Thankfully, another opportunity would always present itself.
> View image in fullscreen Impossible not to care for them … Jason and Lucia in Grand Theft Auto VI. Photograph: Rockstar GamesI often felt that the only thing messing up Rockstar’s perfect simulation was me. All this detail and realism comes with some disadvantages, namely complex controls and a tendency for the game’s systems to collide with my intentions in unexpected and sometimes annoying ways. Here I am, driving at high speed through the city before clipping the kerb and flipping my car, causing a massive pile-up. Here I am pressing the wrong button and accidentally punching a random passerby rather than greeting them as intended, kicking off a ridiculous skirmish in which I have to knock out half the customers at a restaurant before running from the cops. Here I am again pressing the wrong button at a bike rack and ending up pinned beneath a tumbling row of bicycles. Missions can go south very quickly and for reasons that aren’t always obvious. In every street race I wiped out spectacularly by crashing into something I couldn’t properly see, while my opponents magically recovered from every collision and sped ahead. This can be a frustrating game at times: unpredictable, laborious, unwieldy and, occasionally, unfair. That is because you are not the master of the game world. You simply exist within it.
> Like most compelling crime fiction, Jason and Lucia’s story involves an escalating series of messy events that pull them further and further from where they started, and have you constantly wondering how on earth they’re going to get out of the newest trouble they’re in. To avoid spoilers, substantive discussion of this story can only happen in the coming weeks. But I will say that I was rooting so hard for Jason and Lucia by the end that I felt quite sick with worry about what was going to happen to them, pacing back and forth in front of my TV throughout the final missions. Among all the expectations I had for GTA VI, I did not expect it to make me so emotional.
> View image in fullscreen It’s so easy to get away with crime in this city … the Leonida Keys in Grand Theft Auto VI. Photograph: Rockstar GamesThe key to this is the bond you form with Jason and Lucia. After tens of hours in their company, watching them together – how she smiles fondly at him when they dance together, their playful banter, the stick-ups they pull off as a duo, their resilience and faith in themselves and each other in the face of escalating disaster – I found it impossible not to care for them. They are our avatars in GTA VI’s world but they are not blank stand-ins for the player: you decide their actions but not their personalities. They feel like real people rather than puppets dancing to your whim. It made me care about them much more. When the story gave me opportunities to decide what would happen next, what came to mind for me was what they would do, not what I would do.
> This is indicative of a tonal shift for Grand Theft Auto that became more obvious the more I played. This series is famous for its violence, misanthropy and pitch-black humour. I have been invested in its characters before, have even rooted for some of them, but I have rarely liked them or related to them. This is the first GTA that wants to encourage some measure of empathy alongside its trademark violent chaos. I was astonished to discover that the game offers you small incentives for acts of kindness, such as texting your partner a selfie, doing your neighbour a favour or throwing your rubbish in the bin rather than dropping it on the ground. Jason and Lucia are not extravagant caricatures, but two people trying to make it in a world totally stacked against them. Pretty much everyone in this Floridian fever-dream is a total crook, on the take or mixed up in some bullshit scheme. It’s so easy to get away with crime in this city, and so difficult to do things the right way. The events of this game might be totally outlandish but these characters and their motivations keep things at least somewhat grounded.
> View image in fullscreen Still over-the-top offensive in every imaginable way … Grand Theft Auto VI. Photograph: RockstarKiller tunes: how Grand Theft Auto conquered the music world Read moreIf you thought this newfound heart might tone down GTA’s 18-rated provocativeness, however, you would be very wrong. The protagonists may be surprisingly relatable but they exist in a world that is absurdly foul-mouthed, filthy and over-the-top offensive in every imaginable way. I have never played a game that has more thoroughly earned its 18 rating. Barely a half-hour ever goes by without someone snorting coke off a knife blade, or some full-frontal nudity. There are missions set inside a pornographer’s mansion and a small-town strip club; you can visit those clubs and get a private dance (as either Jason or Lucia, for what it’s worth, or together). At one point Lucia opens the wrong hotel room door to see a woman in a corset wielding a golf club, thwacking balls at a guy’s testicles. On the in-game TV there is a reality show about horny geriatrics. It does not so much push the boundaries of taste as ignore the existence of taste. It contains every perverted scenario you could imagine and several more that would never occur to you.
> Sometimes it is a little jarring to emerge from a really pivotal and moving scene between Jason and Lucia into a virtual city where the billboards read things like “WANTED for shitting everywhere: THE SHIT BEAST.” But I found these two sides of GTA’s personality surprisingly easy to accommodate. It’s not as though the story is without its many moments of absurd levity and humour, too: at one point I was taking a bunch of terrifying gang leaders with face tattoos on a real-estate tour, where they sincerely admired the outdoor space with brick pizza oven, and another time I was chasing a man wearing nothing but an alligator thong through a well-to-do suburban neighbourhood. A game this huge can accommodate both pathos and lewdness, and much more.
> View image in fullscreen Women aren’t always the butt of a joke … Lucia in Grand Theft Auto VI. Photograph: Rockstar GamesI did find, however, that Lucia – Grand Theft Auto’s first female protagonist – changed how a lot of this landed for me. GTA has never been particularly kind to women (or men, for that fact, but in past games it has exclusively been the women who were sexualised). There is still a lot of sexism in GTA VI’s world, but now we have Lucia to react to it. This is the first GTA in which I have felt the women are treated as people, not only Lucia but also the many other female characters in the story, from up-and-coming rappers to Lucia’s mother, from a jaded strip-club worker to a badass middle-aged drug-runner whose custom purple carbine rifle is her prized possession. This is a game in which women can be as violent, visibly tough and deeply messed-up as the men. And without wanting to give too much away: there are male strippers in Leonida, too.
> I am not about to make a case for GTA VI as a feminist game – there is much to be offended by here, if you are so inclined – but I will say that as a woman who has played and enjoyed every GTA game while also often rolling my eyes at their casual sniggering misogyny, GTA VI hits different for me. I liked it more because the women aren’t always the butt of a joke. Also for the first time, I did not find the violence gratuitous or overblown, despite the fact that this is a story about crime and criminals. There is nothing here like GTA V’s infamous torture mission, which made me feel sick. It says a lot that of all the immoral opportunities afforded to me in Vice City, the only thing I straight-up said “no” to was getting involved in a metaverse scam. THAT would be going too far.
> View image in fullscreen The game’s most ostentatiously expensive and showy scenarios … a nightclub in Grand Theft Auto VI. Photograph: Rockstar GamesI keep reaching for something that sums up GTA VI, as much as it’s possible to sum up a game as vast as this, and the closest I come is the nightclubs. These show GTA VI at its most extravagant: hundreds of virtual people under the pulsing lights, all dressed up to go out, dancing to a fastidiously curated soundtrack featuring some of the real world’s most famous artists as the controller pulses to the bassline in your hands. These big nights out are an opportunity for both Vice City’s sleaziest denizens and Rockstar’s developers to flash their cash: they are the game’s most ostentatiously expensive and showy scenarios. But at the centre of it all, there are Jason and Lucia, dancing together, focused on each other in the midst of all this chaos and excess.

### AI asked ‘better questions’ than KPMG accountants in pilot audit
- Canonical URL: https://ainewsradar.xyz/news/7342e72076376f8c
- Primary Source: Financial Times (https://www.ft.com/content/5168b3e9-75d0-4be0-9ccd-d327d6b16c05)
- Executive Summary: KPMG UK conducted its first end-to-end AI audit on a FTSE 250 firm, deploying over 100 AI agents under 'Project Exponential' to execute data collection and analysis. While AI demonstrated superior query depth compared to human auditors, the experiment revealed persistent limitations in regulatory mapping requiring human intervention.
- Key Verified Facts:
* [Core Event] Cath Burnet, Head of Audit at KPMG UK (UK audit practice): Deployed 100+ AI agents for a parallel audit of a FTSE 250 company, enabling autonomous data analysis and suggestion of next steps.
* [Root Cause & Mechanism] To test potential for efficiency gains and cost reduction in labor-intensive auditing processes.
* [Key Technical Spec] KPMG launched 'Project Exponential', utilizing 100+ AI agents for parallel audit testing.
* [Key Position & Outlook] The industry is currently in an early validation phase, struggling to balance cost reduction with rigorous compliance.
- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> KPMG has carried out its first AI-based audit of a UK-listed company, saying the technology asked better questions than its own accountants about aspects of its client’s finances and dug deeper into some issues.
> The Big Four firm this year deployed more than 100 AI agents to review the financial statements of an unnamed FTSE 250 company, running the experiment parallel to a conventional audit by its accountants.
> In several cases “the AI was able to go so much deeper” than the regular audit team, said Cath Burnet, KPMG’s UK head of audit, adding that in some situations it had asked “better questions”.
> But in one area of the audit, a human had to intervene after an AI agent failed to match a set of regulations to the company’s documents, she added.
> The project underlines AI’s potential to disrupt the sector by allowing accounts to be checked more quickly and cheaply even as regulators raise concerns about the risks associated with relying on artificial intelligence.
> Audit firms have traditionally billed clients for large teams of junior accountants doing labour-intensive work, supervised by a small number of senior staff.
> KPMG acknowledged there were “clear time-saving opportunities” from AI-based audits but declined to say whether this would in turn reduce fees.
> KPMG International has itself negotiated lower fees from its auditor by arguing that AI will make the work cheaper.
> Rival Big Four accounting firm PwC has also run several “parallel audit” projects to test AI extensively without relying on it, said Andy Hammond, the firm’s global assurance leader.
> Auditors had previously used AI to help perform specific audit tasks, but until now the technology had not been used across all phases of a large UK audit.
> In KPMG’s experiment, codenamed Project Exponential, agents deployed on different parts of the audit worked autonomously with each other and were able to suggest next steps.
> AI agents had gathered data and analysed and documented it before forming draft conclusions and observations for the audit.
> A team built the agents in four months and then had an audit partner “sign off” the experimental audit, which was not relied on by KPMG when it formally signed off on the company’s accounts.
> KPMG declined to disclose the exact size of the team used in its AI-based audit but said that two partners and one director had worked with senior managers and junior staff building and running the agents.
> The Project Exponential team had a “different shape and size” to a traditional audit, Burnet said, but human involvement had remained “critical”.
> Staff set the agents’ objectives, supplied information about the company’s business and previous audits, checked the agents’ work periodically and challenged their conclusions before finalising the audit opinion.
> The project will be expanded to up to 20 larger audits and KPMG hopes to eventually offer AI-based audits to its clients.
> But the required technology was not yet available at the scale needed to run thousands of audits, Burnet said. Some companies may prefer not to use the service, and few currently had “clean” enough data for AI agents to work with, she added.
> The rapid adoption of AI has sparked concerns about whether auditors can adequately oversee work carried out by machines.
> The UK accounting regulator, the Financial Reporting Council, warned this week that using AI could pose a “distinct threat” to auditors’ integrity and independence if they used insights from AI agents to advise their clients. Auditors are restricted from providing advisory services to audit clients.
> “Whatever technology a firm uses, the auditor remains accountable,” said Mark Babington, executive director of regulatory standards at the FRC. “Auditors need to be able to explain how they used it, challenge its outputs and stand behind the evidence.”
> A report from the Centre for Public Interest Audit, a policy and research group for large audit firms, found last month that 23 per cent of company audit committee chairs, who appoint and oversee auditors, had “limited” confidence in AI.
> Concerns included the risk of auditors becoming over-reliant on AI, weakening their scepticism, as well as data security and potential “hallucinations”, where the technology gives false, misleading or fabricated information.
> Burnet said KPMG’s system provided “full visibility and full traceability” of the AI agents’ work, recording their interactions with documents down to individual characters and timestamps. KPMG gave the FRC a high-level overview of its experiment.

### Tencent’s Sales Miss Estimates in Setback for Founder’s AI Push
- Canonical URL: https://ainewsradar.xyz/news/610739ac5c3564ee
- Primary Source: Bloomberg (https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-18/tencent-s-sales-miss-estimates-in-setback-for-founder-s-ai-push)
- Executive Summary: Tencent reported Q3 revenue of 207.3 billion yuan, growing by 8%, which missed analyst projections. Amid mounting competition from Alibaba and ByteDance, co-founder Pony Ma is driving an aggressive internal AI shift, launching the Hy4 model; however, the company faces external headwinds from US restrictions on Chinese access to Southeast Asian data centers for AI training.
- Key Verified Facts:
* [Core Event] Pony Ma (Co-founder, Tencent), Dowson Tong (CEO of CSIG): Revenue missed projections; pursuing aggressive AI integration (Hy4, WorkBuddy) while navigating restrictions on Southeast Asian data centers.
* [Root Cause & Mechanism] To address stagnation in traditional businesses and pivot toward the AI era to compete with Alibaba and ByteDance.
* [Key Metrics] Q3 revenue reached 207.3 billion yuan, reflecting 8% growth, which missed consensus expectations.
* [Industry Impact & Outlook] Geopolitical risks include US restrictions on Southeast Asian data center access, impacting model training efficiency.
- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> Tencent's Sales Miss Estimates in Setback for Founder's AI Push 1 / 1 Tencent's Sales Miss Estimates in Setback for Founder's AI Push Bloomberg News Updated Wed, November 18, 2026 at 4:12 AM CST 4 min read 0700.HK -0.85% BABA -0.02% Trading disclosure The above button links to Coinbase. > The country's social media leader reported revenue rose 8% to 207.3 billion yuan ($31.1 billion) in the September quarter, lower than the average analyst projection. Net income barely grew during the period.
> The tepid results raise questions about billionaire co-founder Pony Ma's efforts to close the gap with longtime rivals Alibaba Group Holding Ltd. (BABA) and ByteDance Ltd. in the AI era. Last week, he called on half of Tencent's 100,000-strong workforce to harness artificial intelligence in search of new growth avenues, while urging the rest try to boost efficiency in its gaming and social media businesses.
> Tencent has claimed a spate of early successes in its AI push, releasing an Hy4 model this month that it said ranks among China's most powerful. Its WorkBuddy office tool claimed 32 million monthly active users in September, more than its direct rivals combined. At the helm of those efforts is Dowson Tong, one of Ma's key lieutenants, who is driving teams to experiment with products.
> Ma slammed Tencent's AI endeavor as "a leaky ship" in May, then gathered employees at a company anniversary celebration this month where he urged them to contribute more. "If you don't embrace the ongoing intelligence revolution, you get disrupted. This is a matter of life and death," Ma said, according to a transcript of his remarks published by Tencent.
> Competition in China's AI arena is only set to intensify with ByteDance preparing to launch a personal AI assistant and Alibaba planning to spin off its chip unit via an IPO in Hong Kong. Complicating matters, Washington this week unveiled new rules aimed at cutting off Chinese access to Southeast Asian data centers, disrupting a vital avenue for training and developing AI.
> Much of Tencent's hopes now rest on WeChat, the ubiquitous app that's already shouldering much of the monetization burden in areas from advertising to live shopping. WeChat's native agent, Xiaowei, has been in testing since summer. Executives hope it will morph into an AI-first ecosystem that is central to the everyday lives of more than a billion people.
> Chinese big tech firms have shifted toward building out AI data centers and stocking up on scarce chips even as investors increasingly scrutinize the near-term payoffs of such endeavors.
> Tencent's free cash flow turned negative in the June quarter after it hiked capital spending by 180% to $8 billion. That's still on the conservative side compared with Silicon Valley giants like Meta Platforms Inc. and Microsoft Corp.
> Funding a big portion of that spending is Tencent's mainstay games business. The company has become more cautious about starting projects anew during a global industry downturn, while turning to what it calls "evergreen" titles such as Honor of Kings to reap consistent profits.
> In global markets, Path of Exile 2 from a New Zealand studio owned by Tencent is scheduled for a full launch in December after an initial rollout two years ago.
> We don't expect Tencent to generate significant external sales from AI this year, given the monetization challenges in China's fragmented AI sector. The company's AI product lineup — concentrated in office tools, large-language models and coding assistants — isn't sufficiently differentiated from Alibaba and ByteDance, though it should benefit from internal synergies
> --With assistance from Vlad Savov, Luz Ding, Henry Ren and Ville Heiskanen.
> Can Tomatoes Grow in the Desert? A $200 Million Bet That They Can

### Suno's new Visuals feature pairs AI-generated music with AI-generated video
- Canonical URL: https://ainewsradar.xyz/news/2297282a32991c9f
- Primary Source: THE DECODER (https://the-decoder.com/sunos-new-visuals-feature-pairs-ai-generated-music-with-ai-generated-video/)
- Executive Summary: Suno has launched its Visuals feature, utilizing a safety-filtered version of MiniMax’s H3 Move video model to generate synchronized video clips of up to 15 seconds. The feature supports lyric-based lip-syncing and allows users to create content via prompts or reference images, while incorporating mandatory watermarking and copyright filters.
- Key Verified Facts:
* [Core Event] Suno; MiniMax (Web, iOS, and Android platforms): Launched 'Visuals' feature utilizing H3 Move model for 15-second music-synced video generation
* [Root Cause & Mechanism] To expand multi-modal capabilities and mitigate ongoing copyright litigation through embedded watermarking and safety filters
* [Key Technical Spec] Integration of MiniMax's H3 Move model for AI-driven visual production.
* [Official Stance & Demand] Strategic response to ongoing copyright lawsuits and regulatory pressure.
- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> AI music generator Suno can now create images and video clips to go with its songs, thanks to a new feature called Visuals. The feature runs on H3 Move, a customized and safety-filtered version of MiniMax's video model H3. The clips run up to 15 seconds, follow the song's structure, pick up on lyrics, and support lip sync.
> Users can start from a reference photo, a prompt, or one of Suno's preset characters. Lyric videos let you tweak fonts and colors, extend clips on a timeline, and pick the length and aspect ratio. Two quality tiers are available, "Fast"and "Standard."Filters block prompts and uploads that reference specific artists, celebrities, or copyrighted works. Before sharing content outside Suno, the platform adds an embedded watermark.
> Visuals works on the web, iOS, and Android, and requires its own credits. Pro and Premier subscribers get a temporary allotment to try it out.
> In late July, the Munich Regional Court I ruled against Suno in a lawsuit filed by GEMA, Germany's music rights organization, finding copyright infringement. Shortly after, Suno announced tools to label Suno-made songs as AI-generated on other platforms. The company has reached a deal with Warner Music, but Universal and Sony are still pursuing litigation.

### This smell startup says its AI nose is as good as a human’s
- Canonical URL: https://ainewsradar.xyz/news/e031d480ae5815c4
- Primary Source: MIT Tech Review (https://www.technologyreview.com/2026/11/18/1148816/smell-startup-osmo-ai-nose-good-as-humans/)
- Executive Summary: Osmo, founded by former Google Brain researcher Alex Wiltschko, has developed the first foundation model for smell using a proprietary dataset of 10 million human labels and 800 million 'scent tokens'. The model demonstrates human-level proficiency in identifying and synthesizing scents, outperforming professional perfumers in tests conducted by major global consumer goods companies.
- Key Verified Facts:
* [Core Event] Alex Wiltschko, Founder of Osmo (Lab in Newark, New Jersey): Built a foundation model for olfaction using chemical sensor data and human labeling for commercial fragrance design
* [Root Cause & Mechanism] To bridge the data scarcity and industry secrecy in olfactory science through large-scale machine learning
* [Key Metrics] The Gates Foundation, which invested $5 million when Osmo launched, later gave the company a $3.
* [Key Position & Outlook] Future applications target airport security and medical diagnostics.
- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> In a lab near Newark Airport in New Jersey, a team of around 30 experienced human sniffers are slowly working their way through every odor on Earth. Their careful notes—“nutty,” “peachy,” “marine”—are cross-referenced with a chemical analysis to create a rich set of training data for what AI startup Osmo calls the world’s first foundation model for smell. The company’s goal, says founder Alex Wiltschko, is “to give computers a sense of smell.”
> “Scent molecules are really the only language most species on this planet can speak,” he says. “Most species can’t communicate with sound or visually, so it truly is Earth’s original language. And it’s incredibly powerful for us, from a memory and an emotional standpoint. You can smell something once and remember it for the rest of your life. You can smell something on the street and be pulled back to high school.”
> In the last few months, Wiltschko claims, Osmo’s model has achieved “human-level olfactory intelligence.” The company’s definition of this is that the model is about as good as the average person at detecting and discriminating between smells, and about as good as a junior perfume designer at creating them. It says its technology is already being used in the fragrance industry to help brands design and manufacture new scents. Last month, the company says, Osmo’s AI model outperformed in-house perfumers at one of the world’s largest consumer goods companies. Wiltschko believes it could be deployed eventually for threat detection at airports, for example, or diagnosing diseases.
> Wiltschko spun the startup out of his work at Google Brain, the search giant’s former AI research lab, in 2023, and he is running the same playbook as AI startups in other domains: Throw a lot of data at difficult problems, and see what happens. The challenge with scent, Wiltschko says, is that there was a dearth of good data. Before Osmo, there were fewer than 200,000 human descriptions of smells in existing databases, by his count. Plus, the chemical sensor devices needed to collect data are expensive, and the fragrance industry is secretive about its work on olfactory science.
> A lot of the company’s work has been in creating its own dataset of more than 10 million human labels and 800 million “scent tokens,” which describe the exact molecules and concentrations that go into creating specific odors. Osmo uses spectrometers and other chemical sensors, running around the clock, to break down the molecular makeup of everything from fruit and flowers to pantry staples and organs. A team of around 70 trained data labelers in the US and overseas spend their days sniffing things and writing down what they smell like, using a standardized fragrance vocabulary.
> Mapping out scents in this way is throwing out some unlikely parallels. In the same way that changing the order of words can drastically influence the meaning of a sentence, rearranging scent molecules in different proportions can drastically alter the smells humans perceive. “The scent tokens that define the smell of a newborn baby have massive overlap with the scent tokens in a fresh plate of cooked spaghetti,” Wiltschko says. (Specifically Barilla brand spaghetti, he says, which perhaps raises some questions for the people at the pasta factory.)
> The company also creates its own scents, using a smell-printing robot the size of a school bus that mixes ingredients according to precise formulas to make samples for Osmo’s own research and fragrances for paying customers. It can design and print scents to order based on a ChatGPT-style prompt. Wiltschko flipped open his laptop to show me how the AI model worked. He opened a text box on screen, and I asked him to generate a fragrance that smelled like a Portuguese custard tart (we were in Lisbon for Web Summit), aimed at 18- to 23-year-old men. The system spent a few minutes cogitating, then generated three options for potential scent profiles that matched the brief (creamy, coconutty, fruity) and the molecules needed to create them. If I’d continued with the ordering process, my signature L’Eau de Custard would have been ready about a week later.
> Osmo’s technology has already been used to create retail fragrances, including for giants like Procter & Gamble. The Gates Foundation, which invested $5 million when Osmo launched, later gave the company a $3.5 million grant to assess molecules that repel disease-carrying insects, and Osmo identified eight substances that were more repellent than DEET. Osmo has also worked with StockX, the online clothing marketplace, on using smell to spot counterfeit sneakers by detecting differences in the chemical composition of the materials used in the shoes.
> But not everyone is convinced by the technology or the company’s big claims. Avery Gilbert, a smell scientist and author of What the Nose Knows , has been sharply critical of Osmo on his Substack , arguing that some of its marketing claims are undocumented, and that its patent filings still rely on human sensory panels and perfumers, rather than AI. “This heavy reliance on human sensory judgments seems odd for a company premised on super-cool AI,” he wrote in March. A representative for Osmo did not respond in time for publication.
> Michael Schmuker, a former professor of neural computation at the University of Hertfordshire who has previously consulted for Osmo, says the company’s technology is an achievement. With colleagues, he created an open-source, reverse-engineered version of Osmo’s 2023 model, but it lacks the reams of data the company has collected since.
> But even with all this smell data, Osmo may be missing some of the factors that make human olfaction unique, Schmuker says. “Smell is super complex. Context is very important for smell. The same molecule may evoke a different association depending on context,” he says. “[The smell of] a French cheese like Camembert is partly the same molecule as in used nappies. You don’t confuse the two because of the context.”
> In a controlled setting like a fragrance lab, this lack of context may not matter so much. But it could have an impact if Osmo’s technology becomes, as Wiltschko suggests, the “olfactive channel” for AI world models. Imagine a machine that could sniff out spoilage in food on a production line, or detect tumors through smell the way dogs have been trained to do in pilot studies .
> For that to happen, sensor technology will need to get a lot better, Schmuker says. The models will need to keep improving. Medical diagnostics is the biggest prize.
> “There’s a lot of history of companies that have gone directly at that mountain peak and, unfortunately, not been successful, because it is very expensive and it is very difficult,” Wiltschko says. “So what we’re doing is building this foundation at the foothills of all these mountains. We’re sending expeditions up to the mountains, doing explorations, and basically smelling the whole world.”

### Lovable Wants You to Vibe Code Your Dream Job
- Canonical URL: https://ainewsradar.xyz/news/9396d6c89637bc2e
- Primary Source: Wired AI (https://www.wired.com/story/lovable-wants-you-to-vibe-code-a-living/)
- Executive Summary: Lovable CEO Anton Osika and CTO Fabian Hedin announced a strategic pivot for their $13B-valued startup, evolving their 'vibe coding' platform into an automated business management engine. With 80% of users seeking financial gain but only 35% currently monetizing, the company aims to bridge this gap by integrating automated business strategy, web development, and customer retention tools.
- Key Verified Facts:
* [Core Event] Anton Osika (CEO), Fabian Hedin (CTO), and Lovable: Expanding from a code-generation platform to a full-stack automated business operation engine
* [Root Cause & Mechanism] Addressing the gap between 80% user demand for monetization and only 35% actual revenue generation
* [Key Metrics] Monetization challenge: Bridging the gap where 80% of users seek profit but only 35% succeed.
* [Key Position & Outlook] Technical roadmap: Implementing proactive business dashboards, marketing automation, and CRM integration.
- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> I squint my eyes in confusion when Anton Osika asks if I like cakes. The CEO of Lovable was in the middle of explaining how his AI startup, flush with investment cash and recently valued at over $13 billion, is ready to shift its focus after two years. Why does the vibe-coding king care if I like sweet treats? He thinks that if I do, I might be able to vibe code a living out of that.
> The generative AI revolution completely flipped coding. Rather than a niche skill set where humans had to learn how to talk like computers, software development could be done by computers generating code in response to natural-language requests from humans.
> Osika was early to this shift, launching a viral open-source tool in 2023, a precursor to Lovable. His mission? “Reduce barriers to build.” That initial spark ignited what is now one of Europe’s most dynamic startups.
> Tech insiders talked nonstop last year about the transformative power of “vibe coding” that could empower anyone to build their own software. Parents could whip up custom apps to help track demanding club sports schedules. Picky eaters could create dynamic meal plans that adapt to whatever’s in their fridge. Polyamorous people could build software to manage their relationship hierarchies. Whatever random, niche software you can imagine, you can build it.
> But Osika isn’t satisfied with helping millions of people vibe code apps for their everyday life—he also wants Lovable users to make more cash. The startup claims that around 80 percent of users arrive at the platform with a financial incentive, like building customer-facing platforms for online sales. That said, Lovable also reports that only 35 percent currently earn revenue with their projects.
> That brings us back to the cake question. Lovable’s plan for next year is to help you run a small business based on your passions, like opening a cake shop. Fabian Hedin, Lovable’s other cofounder and chief technology officer, says the startup is building automations to help with everything from initial business strategy and website creation to long-term customer retention and marketing plans.
> For example, a cake shop owner receives an AI-generated morning briefing through a chatbot-style, Lovable dashboard. “You set some goals, and then the AI is proactive in helping you reach those goals,” Hedin says. This briefing analyzes the number of cake boxes sold through a holiday promotion, customer emails it automatically answered, and reminders to make financial deposits on time.
> Lovable has been a boon for savvy social media content creators, who can leverage their platforms better through vibe-coded sites. “People who have audiences themselves are building larger businesses around that,” Osika says. He recently went to a dinner in New York with creators, one of whom uses Lovable to help sell their book. Others have used it to help hawk merch.
> Lovable earning the trust of burgeoning entrepreneurs is critical to the success of this new endeavor, though it may be an uphill battle. Vibe-coded projects were notorious for not necessarily being secure and sometimes exposing user data.
> The startup was one of many vibe-coded services that came under fire this year for facilitating user-generated apps that exposed data on the open web. Earlier this month, Lovable revamped its security approach as part of its effort to make sites generated through its platform more secure by default.
> “The moment real people use what you build, security is the product,” Igor Andriushchenko, Lovable’s head of security, tells WIRED. “That's why it's one of the areas we continue investing in the most and why we’ve built it directly into the platform experience.”
> Osika will see Lovable as successful next year if he can help a new wave of entrepreneurs start sustainable businesses. Why just vibe code an app when you can vibe code a living?

### Goldman Backs Fintech Startup Payhawk at $2 Billion Value
- Canonical URL: https://ainewsradar.xyz/news/46fa8222f4022cbc
- Primary Source: Bloomberg (https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-18/goldman-backs-fintech-startup-payhawk-at-2-billion-value)
- Executive Summary: London-based fintech startup Payhawk raised $280 million in a Series C funding round led by Goldman Sachs, reaching a post-money valuation of $2 billion. The company provides enterprise-grade expense, invoice, and procurement management software, aiming to digitize traditional corporate finance workflows.
- Key Verified Facts:
* [Core Event] Payhawk, Goldman Sachs (Fintech and enterprise SaaS market): Raised $280M Series C at a $2B valuation
* [Root Cause & Mechanism] Driven by global enterprise digital transformation and demand for streamlined cross-border financial management
* [Key Metrics] Payhawk secured $280M in Series C funding led by Goldman Sachs.
* [Key Position & Outlook] The deal highlights capital interest in automated cross-border financial management solutions.
- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> AI-native spend management platform Payhawk has announced US$280m in Series C funding led by Growth Equity of Goldman Sachs Alternatives, bringing its valuation to US$2bn and total funding to more than US$515m.
> Payhawk says the Series C capital will be used to pursue building “the global Finance Operating System for the AI era”.
> “The US$280m we’ve secured will help us scale globally,” Hristo Borisov, Co-Founder and CEO of Payhawk, tells FinTech Magazine.
> “With fintech representing only a small percentage of the global payments market, we, like our investors, see an incredible growth opportunity and room to bring finance teams AI-native products that combine agents, payments infrastructure and enterprise controls."
> Payhawk was founded in 2018 with the AI to transform how businesses handle spending and payments.
> In 2026, it operates across 33 countries and 12 offices, with a platform spanning multiple currencies, banking systems payment rails, regulations and local practices.
> It is this complexity that Hristo believes can become a global advantage: “Europe does not need to build local versions of categories invented somewhere else,” he says.
> “We should build categories the rest of the world follows as craftsmanship and innovation are strongly embedded cultural traits for Europeans.”
> The ultimate aim, Hristo says, is to build the infrastructure through which global businesses run their financial operations, with AI at the forefront.
> “Being born in Europe has exposed us to this complexity from day one. We know what it takes for our customers to stay in control with their businesses spread around the world while scaling and while trying to be efficient at the same time,” Hristo adds.
> “The window to define that category is open now, and we are moving fast.”
> With Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, the ERP systems, banks, treasury products, procurement platforms, travel tools and spend platforms are all becoming more intelligent.
> Yet Payhawk argues that smarter applications do not automatically translate to a smarter finance operation on the whole.
> “Integrations connect systems. MCP makes information easier to access. But an operating system changes how the entire finance function works,” Hristo points out.
> “As software moves from recommending actions to actually taking them, that distinction becomes much more important.”
> That is why Payhawk is building its Finance Operating System around three interconnected layers which allow AI to move beyond simple assistance and become part of the operating model of finance.
> The layers include AI agents which perform financial work, payments infrastructure allowing for agents to safely interact with money, and enterprise controls that provide finance teams with governance on what agents can do and when human assistance is needed.
> Payhawk says this will align its growth while still allowing its customers to save money instead of incentivising them to spend more.
> The independence will also allow Payhawk to develop its AI-native finance suite that work beyond its own cards.
> “Payhawk’s exceptional growth reflects the strength of its engineering DNA, global footprint and clear vision for the future of modern spend management systems,” James Hayward, Managing Director within Growth Equity at Goldman Sachs Alternatives, says.
> “As payments, AI and enterprise software increasingly converge, we believe Payhawk is well positioned to emerge as a leader in this rapidly evolving market.
> “We are excited to partner with the team as they continue to scale globally and enter their next phase of growth.”
> James is set to join Payhawk’s Board of Directors following the Series C funding round.
> Visa partners with Payhawk as its card network, with Payhawk operating as a Visa principal member under EU and UK electronic money institution licences. That status underpins Payhawk’s corporate Visa cards, which sit alongside its expense management, accounts payable, budgeting and procurement tools in a single platform for finance teams.
> Oracle NetSuite integrates with Payhawk through a native connector available on the NetSuite SuiteApp Marketplace. Payhawk reports that 99.7% of transactions sync with zero manual intervention and that customers close their books 50% faster. The link gives enterprise finance teams live, two-way data flow with their ERP.
> Sage Intacct lists Payhawk as a recommended solution on its marketplace following the integration’s launch on 10 September 2024. Multi-entity finance customers can connect all legal entities to Sage Intacct in a single setup, which supports Payhawk’s push into international markets.

### Anthropic IPO set to deliver windfall to handful of smaller VC firms
- Canonical URL: https://ainewsradar.xyz/news/8021e3973f7a24b8
- Primary Source: Financial Times (https://www.ft.com/content/a3430f0d-0080-4970-8eec-2c14c8438b3d?accessToken=zwAAAaHtopUSkdOjQw8NAIBJcNOO7CwUyEOLPQ.MEUCIF1q7aLCnP63ba_HSXgJrufMSFKbE0XM6j8UzDPK2UaJAiEAwlWU3Tct7FROgNE7x9sr3LUUt1DjFS0mZu406msl96Y&sharetype=gift&token=a97c7641-a9cb-433e-a6b6-ea4083f6a825)
- Executive Summary: AI startup Anthropic is preparing for its IPO with an expected valuation of $1.4 trillion, set to deliver over $100 billion in combined returns to early-stage venture capital firms including Spark Capital and Factorial Funds. Post-IPO, Amazon and Google will collectively control nearly 30% of the company, while major investors like Iconiq Capital, Lightspeed Ventures, and Menlo Ventures see their stakes reach multi-billion dollar valuations.
- Key Verified Facts:
* [Core Event] Anthropic, Amazon, Google, Spark Capital, Iconiq Capital: Initiating an IPO at a $1.4 trillion valuation, triggering massive returns for early investors
* [Root Cause & Mechanism] High cost of AI infrastructure and aggressive market pricing for generative AI leaders
* [Key Metrics] Anthropic targets a $1.4T IPO valuation, triggering over $100B in returns for early backers.
* [Official Stance & Demand] The IPO reorders VC influence, centralizing capital toward firms strategically aligned with hyperscalers.
- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> Anthropic’s initial public offering on Thursday will reorder Silicon Valley’s power rankings, with a small group of venture capitalists who bet early and aggressively on the AI lab set for a combined windfall of well over $100bn.
> Anthropic is expected to be valued at $1.4tn or more when it lists. That would be about 2,300 times its value when Anjney Midha — an angel investor and founder of AMP PBC — first backed the company in 2021.
> His firm is among a handful of lesser-known groups primed for massive returns at multiples that would surpass those of larger, blue-chip rivals. Others include Spark Capital, which would own about $11bn of stock at a $1.4tn valuation, and Factorial Funds, which would own just over $10bn, according to FT calculations.
> Spark’s Yasmin Razavi and Factorial’s Sol Bier invested in Anthropic’s series C funding round, which closed in 2023, when the company was valued at about $4bn. Razavi sits on Anthropic’s board.
> Meanwhile, the manager of pop superstar Madonna, Guy Oseary, stands to net more than $7bn from an early investment of just over $400mn.
> “The deck chairs are shifting around in the VC landscape,” said a partner at one midsized VC firm which stands to make billions of dollars. “The leaders in the AI wave are not the same as they were in the previous waves. Different firms are moving up the leaderboard, and we’re glad to be among them.”
> Amazon and Google, which have provided investment and computing resources to Anthropic, will collectively own close to 30 per cent of the company after the IPO.
> The largest financial investor in the company, Iconiq Capital, holds a fraction of that. Nevertheless, its stake would be worth about $28bn at a $1.4tn valuation. It is followed by Lightspeed Ventures — which has invested roughly $3.2bn for a stake worth just over $25bn at the same valuation — and Menlo Ventures, which stands to return $21bn from an initial $1bn investment.
> Coatue and Singapore’s sovereign wealth fund GIC invested later but went big. The pair led a funding round earlier this year which valued Anthropic at $380bn, and have each put close to $5bn into the company. Those stakes would be worth more than $10bn at an IPO price of $1.4tn.
> Sound Ventures, which was founded by Oseary and actor Ashton Kutcher, and Bessemer Venture Partners are each poised for returns of about $7bn. For Bessemer, that would mark an eightfold increase on its initial investment, while Sound stands to make roughly 17 times its outlay.
> Even those massive multiples are dwarfed, though, by the roughly 70-times return jailed crypto exchange founder Sam Bankman-Fried would have made if his company had not been forced to sell its $500mn stake in bankruptcy proceedings in 2024. That stake would be worth about $35bn at an IPO price of $1.4tn.
> The clamour to own a stake in the AI company has increased in the past year, as the group’s revenues have leapfrogged rival OpenAI. A partner at one of Anthropic’s large investors said they “wrote [chief financial officer Krishna Rao] a love letter” as they jostled for access to a funding round earlier this year.
> The take-off prompted OpenAI’s investors, including Brad Gerstner’s Altimeter, Sequoia Capital and Peter Thiel’s Founders Fund, to pour money into Anthropic, an unusual move in Silicon Valley, where VCs tend to back a single company in each field and founders prize fealty.
> Other big-name venture firms, including Thrive Capital and Andreessen Horowitz, skipped Anthropic entirely.
> “Call us old school . . . but we are serial monogamists,” said Josh Kushner, founder of Thrive, which is one of OpenAI’s largest and most vocal backers, in a since-deleted post on X.
> Andreessen’s partners and Anthropic’s executives, meanwhile, have clashed over how best to regulate AI.
> A successful IPO would also make thousands of Anthropic employees multimillionaires.
> However, the company’s executives have framed fundraising as a necessary evil in the pursuit of their mission to responsibly “develop advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity”.
> While its investors celebrate once-in-a-lifetime returns, Anthropic’s leadership is plotting a low-key IPO. The company has no plans for a party to celebrate the listing and intends to keep fanfare around what is set to be the biggest listing fundraise of all time to a minimum, said people with knowledge of the matter.

### Copilot is “the new OS for work,” and now Office runs inside of it
- Canonical URL: https://ainewsradar.xyz/news/31baf07afe5b3960
- Primary Source: Ars Technica (https://arstechnica.com/gadgets/2026/11/microsoft-calls-copilot-the-new-os-for-work-at-ignite-keynote/)
- Executive Summary: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella announced the general availability of Word, Excel, and PowerPoint within Copilot at Ignite, shifting traditional software apps into secondary plugin components for AI Agents. The launch also introduces Copilot Autopilot, an autonomous agent for cross-service task delegation, powered by the new Work IQ organizational intelligence platform.
- Key Verified Facts:
* [Core Event] Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella (Microsoft Ignite Conference): Integrated Office apps into Copilot, launched Copilot Autopilot and Work IQ
* [Root Cause & Mechanism] Transforming legacy apps into support layers for autonomous AI agents to drive productivity
* [Key Fact Detail] Product paradigm shift: Office apps relegated to backend plugins, moving from tools to AI-driven services.
* [Key Position & Outlook] Market and compliance: Consumption-based billing via Copilot Credits; requires internal IT data governance audits.
- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> Opening the keynote at its Ignite event, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella outlined the company’s vision for its new “frontier ecosystem,” announcing Tuesday the general availability of Word, Excel, and PowerPoint inside Copilot, which he described as “the new OS for work.”
> The announcement is a striking inversion of how we’ve traditionally used software. Rather than an app like Word being the attraction and Clippy the assistant to help you use it, Microsoft envisions the new Copilot integrations will see agents driving things, with the software packages riding shotgun. Applications will become plugin components of the agent’s work, backed by an organizational knowledge layer that draws context from emails, meetings, calendars, chats, and files. Users will now be able to create documents, spreadsheets, and presentations directly in Copilot, with the resulting files remaining editable in their respective Office applications.
> The rollout marks a major step toward the Copilot redesign the company first announced in September. Parts of that vision are now becoming “generally available,” as Nadella puts it, with autonomous agents and new governance tools arriving alongside them.
> ### All about agents
> Copilot Autopilot (not to be confused with Windows Autopilot) is a “persistent, proactive agent for personal productivity” according to Microsoft. In a nutshell, Autopilot is a cloud-based autonomous AI agent that users can delegate responsibilities to, not just single tasks. Autopilot can be authorized to work across services like email and calendars and complete tasks assigned to it as part of its role. Autopilot will use usage-based billing via Copilot Credits, but final pricing has not been announced ahead of general availability.
> Also announced as generally available at the keynote speech was Microsoft IQ, an intelligence platform that houses Work IQ, a context layer that helps agents understand a company’s communications, relationships, and ongoing work. Nadella described Work IQ as perhaps a company’s most valuable database: “It has a deep understanding of the people, their relationships to other people, your emails, your meetings, chats, projects that make up all the fabric of work.” Whether companies want autonomous agents to have access to internal documents and messaging data will have to be determined by their own internal IT review.
> Copilot Workspaces is a collaborative environment currently available through Microsoft’s Frontier early-access program, but coming soon will be the ability to bring personal Autopilot agents into Workspaces. Early in the keynote address, Nadella said that “Until now, AI interactions have mostly been single-player. Workspaces makes it a truly multiplayer experience, where people and agents drive towards a common goal, with shared context.”
> ### Governance over trust
> Trust, the third pillar of Microsoft’s new frontier ecosystem, was something that Nadella continued returning to during his presentation, and not in a way that some might expect. “We find ourselves in a place where alignment is elusive. Mechanistic understanding of these models is elusive. The question is: How can you even trust all this powerful technology? The reality is, by definition, you can’t,” he said.
> In a departure from the norms of “AI is magic” corporate hype sentiment, Nadella conceded that the internal workings of AI thought processes remain difficult to understand, and models cannot be trusted to govern themselves, regardless of whether their answers are accurate. Nadella described the solution as “an architectural imperative to separate the supply of intelligence” from the authority granted to it. Microsoft says each Autopilot agent will have a unique ID, and administrators can restrict permissions or block it entirely. All agent activities are logged for human review, and Autopilot can ask for human approval before engaging in certain actions.
> The promised agent controls and admission that AI systems can’t always be trusted are meaningful, but Microsoft is asking businesses and users to place their trust in the company’s own safeguards instead, though the effectiveness of those safeguards against mistakes, rogue actions, or data exposure will still have to be demonstrated. In Microsoft’s view, the solution to untrustworthy intelligence is not to make AI agents trustworthy, but to control what they’re permitted to do. Businesses will have to decide how much autonomy they delegate to agents.
> Along with the guardrails, Microsoft announced what it calls the “AI Transparency Initiative.” The effort has partnered with 40-plus major companies, including Adobe and Mastercard, to develop open, industrywide standards for AI governance and security. Nadella described the initiative as a way for industry to “help establish an open standard that makes AI safer, more transparent, and more accessible.”
> ### Minding and measuring token-spend
> Along with the other announced additions, Microsoft also announced expanding capabilities for Agent 365, its existing control plane for managing AI agents across enterprise environments. The new agent sheriff extends existing identity, security, and management systems to AI agents. Microsoft describes the objective as providing “observability at every layer of the stack.” Agent 365 offers governance controls over agent behavior in what Microsoft says is “autonomous in execution, but bounded and supervised.”
> Along with Agent 365 comes Agent 365 Business Analytics: “You can simply think of this as an ERP system of AI usage. You can see exactly what’s driving the spend and connect the spend to the outcomes that drive business value,” said Nadella. Customers will be able to see real-world costs associated with AI token-spend, and compare those metrics to the value of work performed. Microsoft acknowledged that the estimations of assisted work hours are determined by a model, and not a direct measurement of time that may have been saved. This is a telling concession for Microsoft to make as businesses evaluate whether there will be an ROI on AI implementations, but according to Judson Althoff, CEO of Microsoft Commercial Business, “anything you can do with Claude or ChatGPT, you can do better with Copilot, for less.”
> ### The outage in the room
> Nadella offered only a brief acknowledgment of last week’s outage that disrupted access to services like Exchange Online and Teams for users across the globe. “Last week was a reminder of how critical digital infrastructure is as the dial tone for the world,” he said. “We know the trust you place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously, and in that context I know we have work to do.”
> That statement was all the time the elephant in the room was given, but Microsoft did seem to acknowledge the public’s growing concern over data center projects by highlighting the previously discussed “community-first AI infrastructure plan.” Not a surprise in a presentation that asks organizations to extend more autonomy to software agents, at a time when Microsoft’s existing infrastructure is under increased scrutiny.

### Over a Third of Gen Z-ers Rely on AI for Friendship
- Canonical URL: https://ainewsradar.xyz/news/81ddfa434a713576
- Primary Source: Wired AI (https://www.wired.com/story/over-a-third-of-gen-z-rely-on-ai-for-friendship/)
- Executive Summary: A study by Gallup and the Digital Wellness Lab at Boston Children's Hospital surveyed 15,925 youth across 16 countries, finding 33% of Gen Z rely on AI for companionship, peaking at 50% among daily users. While AI fills social gaps, it fails to match the emotional support of in-person bonds, with reliance on digital-only connections correlating with increased loneliness.
- Key Verified Facts:
* [Core Event] Gallup, Digital Wellness Lab at Boston Children's Hospital: Released a study on Gen Z's digital habits and mental health, highlighting the AI companionship trend
* [Root Cause & Mechanism] To analyze the correlation between digital social habits and mental well-being
* [Key Metrics] Prevalence reaches 50% among daily users, linked to higher risk of loneliness.
* [Key Position & Outlook] In-person friendships remain superior for emotional support compared to digital-only modes.
- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> As generational cohorts go, Gen Z has been saddled with its share of labels. They scarcely have sex, are “quiet quitters” when it comes to office jobs, and, as they avoid traditional partnership, have learned to solomaxx.
> Whether these labels are deserved or completely off the mark, what continually connects this unique class of young people is a desire to reconstruct how they think about connection.
> In “Friendship in an Online-Offline World: Digital Life, Connection and Wellbeing” researchers from public polling firm Gallup and the Digital Wellness Lab at Boston Children’s Hospital found that more than one-third of Gen Z (33 percent) rely on AI for companionship. The percentage was higher among daily AI users, spiking to 50 percent, and 42 percent among those with online-only friends.
> Rather than measure the consequences of screen time alone, the report examines who Gen Z connects with and how those relationships not only account for their social lives but also how they impact their mental health. While in-person friendships were rated the highest for “strength and support” and were “associated with the most positive emotional experiences,” young people who rely on online-only friends or AI as a social companion may have higher odds of loneliness than those who do not.
> Researchers examined three modes of what they consider close connection: in-person friendships, friendships that started IRL but are sustained online, and online-only friendships where a young person has never met their friend in real life. The survey, conducted between May and August, sampled 15,925 people aged 15 to 22 across 16 countries, and suggests that Gen Z benefits more from IRL relationships compared to digital ones, despite nearly half of young people in the US having at least one close online-only friend.
> “Adolescence is a time when you thrive when you socialize, and so they’re looking for all of these contexts to socialize in,” says David Bickham, research director of the Digital Wellness Lab. “I don’t necessarily see it as, oh, these kids have some sort of major deficit and are looking to AI. I see it as these are young people who are growing up in a time of AI, the most powerful way to find information online, and the more they use it, they see and are more engaged with the social side of it.”
> While AI may help fill a genuine social gap, it hasn’t yet taken the place of their IRL bonds. “In-person and digitally mediated friendships coexist within the same social life,” write the authors of the report.
> When it comes to maintaining those affiliations, Instagram and Discord—surprisingly, not TikTok—were the top platforms in the US for staying in touch with online-only friends. Bickham also noted that “loneliness specifically may be something that these online relationships can’t quite compensate for.”
> “Kids who are reporting loneliness really do things online that are consistent with trying to make friends. They talk to people they don't know, which is always a risk, but it’s also how you make friends,” Bickham says. The report found that Gen Z men, who were more likely to have digital friendships than women, often encountered new acquaintances through gaming, while young women mentioned social media as their most common category to cultivate connection. “What’s intriguing is that boys who are higher in social anxiety are less likely to make connections. They tend to do things by themselves, but when it comes to AI, what we found is that kids who are still lonely are going to seek out connections” with chatbots, Bickham says.
> Recent debates over teen screen time have centered on whether digital devices are driving a youth mental health crisis or if the concerns are overstated. Some critics believe that by only measuring screen time it overlooks the type of content young people watch. This year, social media bans and age-restriction policies for minors took effect in Australia and the UK. In the US, where state legislators have introduced bills to curb addictive design features, a majority of Americans support banning kids under 16 from using social media, according to a recent Pew Research survey.
> Jon-Patrick Allem, an associate professor at the Rutgers School of Public Health, wrote last year in the American Journal of Preventive Medicine that research on the topic has primarily focused on “blunt measures of screen time” and that doing so would “treat all content consumed online as uniform.” Allem concluded that this approach is “deficient” and called on researchers to set a new agenda that instead investigates the actual content kids were consuming, not just time spent.
> It was also important to Bickham and his team to look beyond a surface-level analysis of screen time and consider the nature of the relationships being formed while young people were online, zeroing in on how that time is spent and who it’s spent with.
> “It’s very difficult to measure screen time accurately in a survey. Mainly because half the kids told us this was something they’re doing all the time. A more important finding is the quality of relationship. It’s how you use these platforms that’s going to dictate your outcome, not just how long you use them for.”
> A previous report from the Digital Wellness Lab mapped the use of AI among teenagers in the US, Brazil, and France and found that teens aged 13 to 17 were turning to AI for personal advice and creative work, in addition to companionship.
> While researchers are wary of classifying the report as a permanent shift in how young people form relationships, they say it does signal a growing reliance on AI companionship as part of a pattern of digital social engagement unfolding among Gen Z.
> “It wouldn’t be surprising if AI companionship becomes more common over the next five years as AI becomes integrated into young people’s everyday lives,” says Andrew Dugan, a principal researcher at Gallup. “But whether young people are turning to AI because they feel lonely, or whether AI companionship might reinforce those feelings, remains an important question for future research.”

### YouTube found a new way to inflate view counts
- Canonical URL: https://ainewsradar.xyz/news/0b15b2be14afb083
- Primary Source: The Verge (https://www.theverge.com/streaming/1035683/youtube-co-views-count)
- Executive Summary: YouTube has introduced 'co-viewing' metrics for TV-based content, including long-form, Shorts, and live streams, by using a privacy-safe statistical model to estimate multiple viewers per device. This move aligns the platform with traditional TV industry standards, relies on demographic data rather than hardware sensors, and does not impact creator monetization.
- Key Verified Facts:
* [Core Event] YouTube: Implemented a co-viewing estimation model to inflate public view counts on TV
* [Root Cause & Mechanism] To align with traditional TV industry viewing metrics and improve reach reporting
* [Key Fact Detail] Co-viewing figures integrated into TV play counts.
* [Industry Impact & Outlook] Neutral impact on creator monetization and revenue eligibility.
- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> YouTube’s view counts will now include the number of people that it estimates are watching a video together on TV. In an update on Monday, the platform says it’s bringing “co-views” to public view counts across long-form videos, Shorts, and live content to provide a more “complete picture” of how people are using its platform.
> YouTube, which has become even more popular on TVs than phones, also says the change will help it align with “TV industry standards,” which similarly record views by estimating the number of people watching shows. The company says it doesn’t use devices, like cameras or microphones, to estimate how many people are watching a video on TV. Instead, it estimates co-views using a “privacy safe statistical model” that takes into account “demographic patterns and viewing times.”
> This marks yet another update to YouTube’s view count system. In August, the platform began counting a view as soon as a video starts playing. The company said at the time that creators will notice their view counts increasing faster as a result of this change, and it seems like adding co-views could boost these numbers as well.
> YouTube notes that it will only apply co-views to new views on TV going forward, and that they won’t appear retroactively. Co-views also won’t affect a creator’s ad revenue, YouTube Partner Program eligibility, or revenue.
